---
title: "Get started"
description: "One dataset, carried through all three packages: structure, folds, models."
---

This is the end-to-end path. It is the one thing no single package site can
show, because every step crosses a package boundary.

The dataset below is deliberately tiny and synthetic so the structure is visible
at a glance: 40 samples, 20 subjects with two samples each, spread across 5
batches. That single fact — two samples per subject — is enough to make a
default 5-fold CV dishonest, because every fold would train on one sample of a
subject and test on the other.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The code on this page was run against splitGraph 0.4.0, bioLeak 0.3.8 and
fastml 0.7.5. It is shown rather than executed at build time so the site does
not carry the full modelling dependency stack. For runnable, output-bearing
versions, see `vignette("quick-start", package = "splitGraph")`,
`vignette("bioLeak-intro", package = "bioLeak")`, and the
[fastml tutorial](https://selcukorkmaz.github.io/fastml-tutorial/).
:::

## 0. Setup

``` r
library(splitGraph)
library(bioLeak)
library(fastml)

set.seed(1)
n <- 40

meta <- data.frame(
  sample_id  = paste0("S", 1:n),
  subject_id = rep(paste0("P", 1:20), each = 2),
  batch_id   = rep(paste0("B", 1:5), each = 8),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

dat <- data.frame(
  sample_id = meta$sample_id,
  y  = factor(rep(c("case", "ctrl"), n / 2)),
  x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n), x3 = rnorm(n),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
```

Note the separation: `meta` describes how samples relate to each other, `dat`
holds the measurements. splitGraph only ever sees `meta`.

## 1. Describe the structure — splitGraph

``` r
g <- graph_from_metadata(meta, graph_name = "demo")
validate_graph(g)
```

`graph_from_metadata()` auto-detects canonical columns: `subject_id` becomes
`Subject` nodes with `sample_belongs_to_subject` edges, `batch_id` becomes
`Batch` nodes, and so on. Validation runs structural, semantic, and
leakage-relevant checks, each finding carrying a severity.

Now derive what the structure implies for splitting, and emit the spec:

``` r
con  <- derive_split_constraints(g, mode = "subject")
spec <- as_split_spec(con, graph = g)

spec$group_var    # "group_id"    -- the unit that must not be split
spec$block_vars   # "batch_group" -- coarser axis that ideally should not straddle a fold
```

Passing `graph = g` enriches the spec with the axes the constraint did not use
as its primary grouping, so a downstream tool can block or stratify on them
without ever touching the graph.

If a Python collaborator needs the same split, this is the handoff point:

``` r
write_split_spec(spec, "split_spec.json")
```

## 2. Build and check the folds — bioLeak

The spec is a sample-keyed table. Join its role columns onto the modelling data:

``` r
sd  <- as.data.frame(spec)
dat <- merge(dat, sd[, c("sample_id", "group_id", "batch_group")], by = "sample_id")
```

Then build folds that respect the grouping the graph derived:

``` r
sp <- make_split_plan(
  dat,
  outcome = "y",
  mode    = "subject_grouped",
  group   = spec$group_var,
  v       = 5,
  seed    = 1
)
```

And — this is the step worth not skipping — confirm the folds actually honour
the axis they claim to:

``` r
check_split_overlap(sp)
#>   fold repeat_id      col n_overlap pass
#> 1    1         1 group_id         0 TRUE
#> 2    2         1 group_id         0 TRUE
#> 3    3         1 group_id         0 TRUE
#> 4    4         1 group_id         0 TRUE
#> 5    5         1 group_id         0 TRUE
```

Zero overlap on every fold. A plain `vfold_cv()` on this dataset would have
shown 20 subjects straddling the train/test boundary.

::: {.gv-scope}
`mode = "combined"` handles several axes at once, taking a `constraints` list of
`list(type = , col = )` entries where the first element drives the folds and the
rest act as exclusion constraints. That is how `spec$block_vars` gets enforced
rather than merely recorded.
:::

### Optional: fit and audit inside bioLeak

If the split policy itself is what you are studying, stay in bioLeak — it fits
with train-only preprocessing and then produces evidence:

``` r
fit <- fit_resample(
  dat[, c("x1", "x2", "x3")],
  outcome = dat$y,
  splits  = sp,
  preprocess = list(
    impute    = list(method = "median"),
    normalize = list(method = "zscore")
  ),
  learner = "glmnet"
)

audit <- audit_leakage(fit, metric = "auc", B = 200)
audit_report(audit, file = "audit.html")
```

The imputation and z-scoring are re-estimated inside each training fold. Doing
them once on the full matrix first is the single most common way a clean-looking
pipeline leaks.

## 3. Train and compare models — fastml

Convert the folds to the format the tidymodels world speaks, and hand them over
unchanged:

``` r
rs <- as_rsample(sp, data = dat)
#> <manual_rset> -- 5 splits

model <- fastml(
  data      = dat,
  label     = "y",
  algorithms = c("logistic_reg", "rand_forest", "xgboost"),
  resamples = rs,
  exclude   = c("sample_id", "group_id", "batch_group"),
  seed      = 1
)

summary(model)
```

Two details carry the guarantee:

- `resamples = rs` means fastml uses the folds bioLeak built rather than
  generating its own. The structural work from step 1 survives to step 3.
- `exclude =` drops the identifier and grouping columns from the feature set.
  Leaving `group_id` in as a predictor would hand the model the answer — which
  is target leakage of a particularly embarrassing kind.

Then explain the winner:

``` r
fastexplain(model, method = "dalex")
```

## What each step bought you

| Step | Without it | With it |
|---|---|---|
| splitGraph | The grouping lives in someone's head or a comment | The grouping is an object, validated, and serialisable to JSON |
| `check_split_overlap()` | You assume the folds are clean | You know how many samples straddle each fold |
| Guarded preprocessing | Scaling and imputation see the test fold | They are re-estimated per fold |
| `resamples = rs` | fastml silently resamples from scratch | The upstream structure reaches the model comparison |
| `audit_leakage()` | The AUC is the only number you have | You also have a permutation gap to compare it against |
